## Statement of Need

Literacy is a threshold skill. Without it, adults struggle to read a lease, follow a prescription label, help a child with homework, or advance beyond entry-level employment. In [County], that threshold remains out of reach for a significant share of the population, and the consequences ripple across generations.

According to the [County] Health Department's 2023 community assessment, 18% of adults in the county score below basic on standardized literacy measures — meaning they can perform only the most simple and concrete literacy tasks, if any. That rate is nearly double the statewide average and translates to an estimated [X,XXX] adults who cannot functionally read the documents that govern their daily lives. The problem is not improving. School District data from the 2023–2024 academic year show that 56% of K–8 students are not reading at grade level, suggesting that the pipeline of adults entering the workforce without adequate literacy skills will continue to grow unless intervention reaches both sides of the age spectrum.

**Who is most affected.** The burden falls hardest on residents of [target ZIP codes], where the U.S. Census Bureau (2020) reports a poverty rate of 22%, nearly [X] percentage points above the county median. These neighborhoods are home to large concentrations of immigrants and refugees, working parents without high school credentials, and older adults whose formal education ended early. For these residents, low literacy is not an isolated deficit; it compounds existing barriers to employment, housing stability, healthcare access, and civic participation. Adults who cannot read above a basic level earn, on average, significantly less than their literate peers and are more likely to experience chronic health conditions — outcomes that in turn increase demand on county social services and emergency systems.

**A widening service gap.** Despite the scale of need, [County] has no nonprofit currently offering comprehensive, one-on-one adult literacy tutoring within the target service area. Group classes exist through the community college and one faith-based program, but neither provides individualized instruction, flexible scheduling for shift workers, or instruction that meets learners at pre-literacy levels. The result is a bottleneck visible in our own data: as of [month] 2024, [Organization] maintains a waitlist of 120 adult learners, with an average wait time of six months before a tutor match can be made. Each month on that list is a month in which a parent cannot read to a child, a worker cannot pursue a credential, and a patient cannot interpret discharge instructions.

**Community voice confirms the urgency.** In a 2022 survey of 210 residents across the target ZIP codes, respondents ranked adult literacy as their single highest community concern, above transportation, housing cost, and access to healthcare. Open-ended responses underscored the intergenerational dimension of the problem. One respondent wrote, "[Quote from survey, if available — e.g., 'I dropped out to work, and now my daughter is falling behind too. I can't help her because I can't read what she brings home.']" That sentiment was echoed across age groups and language backgrounds, pointing to a community that recognizes the problem, wants to address it, and lacks the resources to do so on its own.

The data paint a clear picture: a large, growing population of adults and children in [County] cannot read at functional levels; the communities hit hardest are already contending with poverty and limited services; existing programs do not reach the residents most in need; and the community itself has identified literacy as its top priority. Without expanded, individualized tutoring capacity, the cycle will continue — adults will remain on waitlists, children will lose ground, and the county will bear the downstream costs in health, social services, and lost economic productivity.

Literacy is a threshold skill. Without it, adults struggle to read a lease, follow a prescription label, help a child with homework, or advance beyond entry-level employment. For these residents, low literacy is not an isolated deficit; it compounds existing barriers to employment, housing stability, healthcare access, and civic participation. Adults who cannot read above a basic level earn, on average, significantly less than their literate peers and are more likely to experience chronic health conditions — outcomes that in turn increase demand on county social services and emergency systems.

Group classes exist through the community college and one faith-based program, but neither provides individualized instruction, flexible scheduling for shift workers, or instruction that meets learners at pre-literacy levels. Each month on that list is a month in which a parent cannot read to a child, a worker cannot pursue a credential, and a patient cannot interpret discharge instructions.

Community voice confirms the urgency. In a 2022 survey of 210 residents across the target ZIP codes, respondents ranked adult literacy as their single highest community concern, above transportation, housing cost, and access to healthcare. Open-ended responses underscored the intergenerational dimension of the problem. One respondent wrote, "I can't help my kids with homework because I can't read." That sentiment was echoed across age groups and language backgrounds, pointing to a community that recognizes the problem, wants to address it, and lacks the resources to do so on its own.

The data paint a clear picture: a large, growing population of adults and children in Greenville County cannot read at functional levels; the communities hit hardest are already contending with poverty and limited services; existing programs do not reach the residents most in need; and the community itself has identified literacy as its top priority. Without expanded, individualized tutoring capacity, the cycle will continue — adults will remain on waitlists, children will lose ground, and the county will bear the downstream costs in health, social services, and lost economic productivity.

## Section 3: Target Population (~300 words)

LiteracyWorks will serve 360 adults annually through this program. Participants must meet all three of the following eligibility criteria: they must be 18 years of age or older, reside in one of the target ZIP codes within Greenville County, and either have a household income at or below 200% of the federal poverty level or lack a high school diploma or equivalent credential. Within this eligible pool, enrollment priority will be given to parents and primary caregivers of K–8 students, reflecting the intergenerational literacy cycle documented in Section 2 and the community's own emphasis on that connection.

This population reflects the demographics of the target neighborhoods: predominantly low-income, disproportionately people of color, and including a substantial number of immigrants and refugees for whom English is a second or additional language. Many are working adults employed in hourly or shift-based jobs that make it difficult to attend fixed-schedule group classes — precisely the gap LiteracyWorks is designed to fill.

Eligibility will be verified at intake through a brief screening process. Residency will be confirmed by a current utility bill, lease, or piece of mail showing a target ZIP code address. Income will be verified through self-attestation on a standardized form, consistent with the approach used by other federally and state-funded literacy programs in the region; applicants who hold current benefits such as SNAP, Medicaid, or free/reduced lunch for a dependent child will be considered income-eligible automatically. Education status will be confirmed through self-report and, where available, school records. The intake coordinator will document all verifications in the participant file before a tutor match is made.

The 360-person annual target is grounded in LiteracyWorks' current operational capacity and the expansion this grant would fund. It represents a threefold increase over our current enrollment of approximately 120 active learners per year and would eliminate the existing waitlist within the first program year.

## Section 4: Program Design & Activities

**Service model.** LiteracyWorks delivers individualized, evidence-informed one-on-one adult literacy tutoring paired with family supports and flexible delivery options designed to reach working adults and parents who cannot access traditional classroom programs. The model rests on a simple premise supported by decades of adult education research: learners who receive consistent, individualized instruction matched to their starting level and life context make faster and more durable gains than those in large-group-only settings. Studies synthesized by ProLiteracy and the federal LINCS network consistently show that one-to-one and small-group tutoring models produce higher completion rates, stronger literacy gains, and greater learner satisfaction than drop-in or lecture-format programs, particularly for adults reading at the lowest levels. LiteracyWorks builds on that evidence base while adding two elements often missing from volunteer tutoring programs — structured curriculum with progress monitoring and an integrated family literacy component that addresses the intergenerational cycle identified by our community.

**Participant pathway.** Every participant moves through five phases: outreach and referral, intake and assessment, active tutoring, exit assessment, and post-program follow-up. The pathway is designed so that no learner enters services without a baseline measurement and no learner exits without a documented outcome.

In Phase 1, outreach and intake staff identify prospective learners through community canvassing in the target ZIP codes, referral partnerships with Greenville County schools and health clinics, and direct contact with individuals on the existing waitlist. Interested adults complete the intake screening described in Section 3, including eligibility verification, and are assessed using a standardized literacy assessment to establish a baseline reading level. The intake coordinator then develops an individualized learning plan that sets short-term and long-term goals aligned with the learner's own priorities — whether that is reading to a child, passing a GED section, interpreting workplace documents, or navigating digital platforms such as email, job boards, and patient portals.

In Phase 2, the learner is matched with a trained volunteer tutor and begins active instruction. Sessions occur twice per week, 60 minutes each, for a minimum dosage of 96 sessions over approximately 12 months. This dosage reflects research indicating that adults typically need 100 or more contact hours to achieve a measurable level gain on standardized assessments (National Reporting System guidelines; Comings, Sum, and Uvin, 2000). Sessions are delivered in person at LiteracyWorks' learning center, at community sites such as libraries and school buildings, at the learner's home, or via a virtual platform, depending on the learner's work schedule, transportation access, and preference. This flexibility is central to the model; shift workers, parents of young children, and adults without reliable transportation are the residents most likely to fall off waitlists and out of rigid class schedules, and they are the residents who need services most.

The curriculum covers three integrated skill domains. Basic literacy instruction builds decoding, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension using structured, phonics-informed methods appropriate for adult learners. Digital literacy modules teach practical skills such as using email, completing online forms, and navigating job search platforms — skills increasingly required for employment and access to public services. Workplace and family literacy content connects reading practice to the learner's daily context: reading a pay stub, understanding a school notice, following medication instructions, or reading a picture book with a child.

In Phase 3, monthly progress checks using brief formative assessments allow the tutor and program coordinator to adjust the learning plan, increase or decrease session intensity, and address barriers to attendance. Learners who complete the program receive an exit assessment using the same standardized tool administered at intake, producing a comparable pre-post measure.

In Phase 4, follow-up contacts at 3 and 12 months after exit track retention of gains and life outcomes such as employment, further education enrollment, and reading activity with children.

Running alongside the tutoring pathway, LiteracyWorks conducts monthly family literacy workshops for parents enrolled in the program and their K–8 children. Each workshop pairs a child-focused reading activity led by a trained facilitator with a parent coaching session that equips caregivers with strategies to support reading at home. These sessions reinforce the tutoring curriculum, strengthen the parent-child literacy connection flagged by residents in the 2022 community survey, and create peer support among adult learners.

**Tutor recruitment, training, and quality.** Volunteer tutors complete a standardized 12-hour initial onboarding covering adult learning theory, the LiteracyWorks curriculum, cultural responsiveness, and use of progress monitoring tools. After onboarding, tutors receive monthly group coaching sessions and have access to a library of structured lesson plans so that instruction remains consistent and evidence-aligned regardless of individual tutor background. The program coordinator observes sessions quarterly and reviews progress data to ensure fidelity.

**Program management and continuous improvement.** The program coordinator convenes quarterly reviews with staff, tutor leads, and partner organizations to examine enrollment, attendance, assessment, and learner feedback data. Findings from these reviews feed directly into program adjustments — for example, adding evening session slots if attendance data show that daytime hours are a barrier, or revising a curriculum module if formative assessments reveal a consistent skill gap. This feedback loop ensures the program remains responsive to learner needs throughout the grant period.

**Staffing and timeline overview.** Implementation will require a program coordinator (1.0 FTE), an intake and outreach specialist (1.0 FTE), a data and case management assistant (0.5 FTE), and a family literacy facilitator (0.5 FTE), supported by an estimated 60–80 active volunteer tutors at steady state. A detailed staffing table and quarterly milestone timeline are provided in Section 5. Key start-up milestones include completing staff hiring by month 1, launching tutor recruitment and training in months 1–2, beginning learner intake in month 2, and matching the first cohort of tutors and learners by month 3.

## Section 6: Outcomes & Objectives

LiteracyWorks distinguishes between outputs — the volume of services delivered — and outcomes — the measurable changes those services produce in participants' lives. The following objectives are structured accordingly and are designed to be specific, measurable, and verifiable using the data collection methods detailed in Section 7.

**Output objectives.**

By the end of the 12-month grant period, LiteracyWorks will enroll and provide one-on-one tutoring services to 360 adults meeting the eligibility criteria described in Section 3. Of those enrolled, 80% (288 learners) will attend at least 75% of their scheduled sessions, reflecting meaningful engagement with the program rather than intake alone. These two metrics establish that the program is reaching its intended population at sufficient dosage to produce learning gains.

**Primary learning outcome.**

By program exit, 60% of participants will achieve a measurable gain of at least one educational functioning level as measured by the Tests of Adult Basic Education (TABE 11/12) and reported according to National Reporting System (NRS) standards. The one-level gain threshold is the standard benchmark used by federally funded adult education programs and represents a meaningful, life-relevant improvement in reading ability — for example, moving from a level at which a learner can recognize common words and simple sentences to a level at which they can read and interpret short everyday texts such as a bus schedule, a medicine label, or a child's school notice. Baseline for each participant will be established through TABE administration at intake, with the same form series administered at exit to produce a comparable pre-post measure.

**Parent confidence outcome.**

Among participants who are parents or primary caregivers of K–8 students, 70% will report increased confidence and ability to help their child with homework by program exit, as measured by a pre-post learner survey administered at intake and again at the final session. This outcome directly addresses the intergenerational literacy cycle that residents identified as their top concern in the 2022 community survey and that the family literacy workshops are designed to reinforce.

**Employment and education outcome.**

Within 12 months of program exit, 25% of participants who were not employed at intake will have obtained employment or enrolled in a credential, ESL, or GED program. This outcome captures the longer-term economic impact of improved literacy and is measured through follow-up contact at 3 and 12 months post-exit, using participant self-report supplemented by documentation where available.

**Cost-effectiveness.**

LiteracyWorks will report cost per participant served and cost per measurable learning gain (defined as one NRS level increase) in its final report to the funder. These figures will be calculated from actual expenditures and outcome data at year end and will allow comparison with published benchmarks for adult literacy programming. Preliminary estimates will be provided in the budget narrative (Section 8).

Together these objectives create a chain of accountability that runs from enrollment through engagement, learning, family impact, and economic mobility — mirroring the logic model attached to this application and the theory of change described in Section 4.

---

## Section 7: Evaluation Plan

**Purpose and approach.** The evaluation serves two functions: accountability to the funder through rigorous outcome measurement, and continuous improvement through timely data that allows LiteracyWorks to adjust programming during the grant period rather than only at its conclusion. The design is a single-group pre-post model with follow-up, using standardized instruments and consistent data collection points across all participants. While a randomized comparison group is not feasible given the ethical and practical constraints of denying services to waitlisted adults, the use of a nationally normed assessment instrument (TABE 11/12) and NRS-aligned reporting standards allows LiteracyWorks' results to be compared against national benchmarks for adult education programs.

**Data collection instruments and schedule.**

The evaluation relies on four complementary data sources, each tied to specific objectives.

The TABE 11/12 is the primary assessment instrument. It is a nationally normed, NRS-approved standardized test of reading, math, and language skills widely used in adult education programs across the country. LiteracyWorks will administer the reading subtest at two required points — intake and program exit — to produce a pre-post comparison for every enrolled learner. The same form series will be used at both points to ensure comparability. For learners who exit the program early, an exit TABE will be administered at the point of departure so that partial gains can be captured. TABE results will be scored and translated into NRS educational functioning levels by the data and case management assistant, who will be trained in TABE administration and scoring protocols during staff onboarding.

Attendance logs will be maintained by tutors for every scheduled and completed session, recorded in the program's client tracking database within 48 hours of each session. These logs will document session date, duration, location or delivery mode (in-person, virtual, or home-based), and a brief content note. Attendance data will be used to calculate the retention metric (75% attendance threshold) and to analyze the relationship between dosage and learning gains.

A learner survey will be administered at intake and exit to all participants who are parents or primary caregivers of K–8 students. The survey will include Likert-scale items measuring self-reported confidence in helping children with homework, frequency of reading activities at home, and perceived barriers to supporting children's learning. The survey will be available in English and Spanish, with oral administration offered for learners whose reading level would make written completion unreliable. The pre-post change in survey scores will be used to assess the parent confidence outcome.

Employment and education verification will be collected through structured follow-up contacts at 3 and 12 months after program exit. The intake and outreach specialist will contact participants by phone, text, or in person to document current employment status, any new enrollment in a credential, ESL, or GED program, and any other self-reported life changes. Where possible, participants will be asked to provide supporting documentation such as a pay stub, offer letter, or enrollment confirmation. Self-report will be accepted when documentation is not available, consistent with standard practice in community-based adult education evaluation. **Analysis and reporting.** The data and case management assistant will maintain all participant records in a secure, password-protected database. The program coordinator will review aggregate data quarterly as part of the quality improvement cycle described in Section 4, examining enrollment, attendance trends, early TABE results, and learner feedback to identify needed program adjustments. **Data quality and privacy.** All participant data will be collected and stored in compliance with applicable privacy regulations. Informed consent for data collection and follow-up contact will be obtained at intake. TABE administration will follow the publisher's standardized protocols to ensure scoring validity, and the program coordinator will conduct periodic audits of data entry for accuracy.

**Limitations.** LiteracyWorks acknowledges two limitations of this evaluation design. First, the absence of a control or comparison group means that observed gains cannot be attributed solely to the program; maturation, outside learning, and other factors may contribute. The use of a nationally normed instrument and comparison to NRS benchmarks partially mitigates this limitation. Second, post-exit follow-up at 3 and 12 months is dependent on successful recontact, and attrition from follow-up is common in this population. LiteracyWorks will collect multiple forms of contact information at intake and will track follow-up response rates to allow the funder to assess the completeness of post-exit data.
